description: SoughtOut Beyond is my NASA Space Apps project exploring the stories of machines humanity left on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. I’m an Electrical & Computer Engineering student passionate about robotics, AI, autonomous systems, and space exploration, with experience in UAV research, ROS 2, C/C++, Python, and simulation.
summary:
SoughtOut Beyond is an interactive website that tells the stories of 16 machines humanity left behind on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space, from the Apollo 11 laser reflector to the Ingenuity helicopter and Pioneer 10. Each machine speaks in its own voice and guides students through five short chapters: why it was sent, how it got there, what it discovered, how its mission ended, and why it still matters. A 3-question quiz follows, with every answer found in the story. A map built on NASA's Moon and Mars maps shows where each machine rests, and Scout, a 3D guide made from parts of real machines, leads readers through the site.

It answers the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge by turning scattered technical mission pages into stories that school-age space fans can enjoy and remember. Every fact is checked against NASA, JPL, and NSSDCA pages, which are listed at the end of each story. It is free to use in any browser and includes read-aloud, larger text, high contrast, and printable worksheets for teachers. These machines were left behind, but they are not forgotten.
details:
What it does

SoughtOut Beyond tells the stories of 16 machines people left on the Moon, on Mars and out in deep space. You start with a catalog of all of them. Pick one, say Opportunity, and it talks to you: "My job was 90 days and about one kilometer. I drove 45." Then it walks you through five short chapters (The Mission, The Journey, The Discovery, The Final Signal and The Legacy) and finishes with a 3-question quiz. I made sure every quiz answer is somewhere in the story, so nobody gets tested on something they weren't told.

There's more to explore too. A map shows where each machine stopped for good, plotted by latitude and longitude on NASA's Moon and Mars maps, and tapping a dot opens that machine's story. There's a timeline of how long each one worked, and a counter that keeps ticking up the days since Opportunity last called home. And there's Scout, a 3D robot I built out of parts from real machines: Opportunity's cameras, the prisms from the Apollo 11 laser mirror, Pioneer 10's dish. You can spin Scout around, pull the parts off, and tap each one to meet the machine it came from. Scout also shows you around the site.

Why it matters

Most people don't know these machines are still sitting out there. When I looked them up, the information was all there on NASA's sites, but it was written for scientists. I wanted something a 10-year-old could read on a phone and remember the next day. It's free, there's no sign-up, and teachers can print any story as a worksheet with the quiz, the answers and the sources.

Where the idea came from

The name comes from Isaiah 62:12: "thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken." That's how I think about these machines. They were left behind, but they aren't forgotten, so I went looking for them.

What I thought about while building it

Getting the facts right came first. Everything is checked against NASA, JPL or NSSDCA pages (23 of them), and each story lists its sources. I also wanted everyone to be able to use it, so there's read-aloud, a larger-text mode, high contrast, keyboard support and image descriptions. Nobody has to make an account, and progress is only saved in your own browser. And I was upfront about AI: the AI-made background pictures are labelled on the page, and the footer explains how I used AI.

What I used

TypeScript, React, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion for animation, three.js for the 3D Scout, the browser's built-in speech for read-aloud, and GitHub Pages to host it. I used Claude Design to plan the look, Claude to help me write the code, and Higgsfield for the background pictures.
